title: Big Investors Hunt for Tomorrow's AI Winners as Capex Fears Fade
excerpt: Asset managers are doubling down on hyperscalers while warning that neocloud providers face a reckoning as the AI market matures.
body:
• Major asset managers are shifting AI bets from chipmakers alone toward hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, whose scale and customer relationships offer lasting advantages.
  • Despite a July semiconductor rout and rising Chinese competition, Wellington Management ($1.3 trillion AUM) has increased its hyperscaler positions, calling them "very large beneficiaries" of the AI paradigm shift.
  • A Reuters analysis estimates hyperscalers will generate $340 billion more in annual operating cash flow by 2027, though capex is expected to rise by roughly $534 billion over the same period.
  • Neocloud providers like CoreWeave and Nebius have surged 50% and 200% respectively, but analysts warn they could be vulnerable if new capacity normalizes pricing.

The rally in AI-linked stocks during the latest earnings season has shifted the investment narrative from whether Big Tech's spending spree will pay off to a sharper question: which companies will deliver returns over the long term?

Results from Microsoft and Amazon reassured markets last week that demand remains robust for the infrastructure underpinning artificial intelligence. Cloud growth is accelerating, and capacity constraints persist — conditions that have prompted some of the world's largest asset managers to rethink their positioning across the AI ecosystem.

Hyperscalers Gain Favor as Core Holdings

Many institutional investors retain significant positions in semiconductor stocks even after a sector rout in July, when doubts set in over whether AI spending was justified and competition from Chinese chipmakers intensified. But the emphasis is shifting.

"The hyperscalers are being recognised in this moment as companies that are likely to be very large beneficiaries of this AI paradigm shift. They remain core holdings in our portfolios, and we've in fact increased our positioning in many of these companies recently."

— Brian Barbetta, Co-head of Technology, Wellington Management

Wellington Management, which oversees about $1.3 trillion in assets, has added exposure to the biggest cloud service providers — Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta — whose scale allows them to rapidly expand AI infrastructure to meet customer demands.

Richard Clode, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson's Bankers Investment Trust, echoed the sentiment. Amazon is one of his fund's biggest overweight positions. "Today's capex is tomorrow's sales," Clode told Reuters.

The Math Behind the Mega-Spending

The four biggest AI capex spenders — Microsoft, Amazon, Google parent Alphabet, and Meta — all lagged a 75% surge in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index this year. They also trailed gains by Nvidia-backed neocloud providers CoreWeave, up around 50%, and Nebius, up over 200%.

Yet the longer-term case for hyperscalers is building. A Reuters analysis estimates they will generate about $340 billion more in annual operating cash flow in 2027 than in 2025. Capex, however, is expected to rise by roughly $534 billion over the same period — meaning the spending gap will take time to close.

Clode argues the inflection is near. "By later next year into 2028, we think you're going to start seeing these companies growing profits and cash flow faster than the incremental capex growth," he said.

Not Chips Versus Cloud — Both

John Lamb, equity investment director at Capital Group, which manages about $3.6 trillion, cautioned against framing the AI opportunity as a binary choice. "It's not about whether chips are better investments than hyperscalers. It's about having both in your portfolio," he said, noting that data centres typically take 12 to 18 months to move from construction to producing revenue.

The latest quarterly earnings represent "this inflection point," Lamb added, where infrastructure investments are beginning to generate returns.

Neoclouds Face a Reckoning

While neocloud providers have capitalised on elevated spot pricing for scarce AI computing capacity, their model carries risks. BCA Research Chief U.S. Equity Strategist Noah Weisenberger said these companies could be vulnerable if new computing capacity comes online and pricing normalizes, given their heavier reliance on debt and high pricing.

Weisenberger recommends a long-hyperscalers, short-neoclouds trade, arguing that Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have more lasting advantages because of their scale and deep customer relationships.

Can Spending Be Justified?

Even for the winners, challenges remain. Swiss wealth manager LGF+ZEST CIO Alberto Conca estimates AI monetisation needs a fivefold to thirteenfold increase to justify current spending plans — a sobering reminder that the market is pricing in outcomes that have not yet materialized.

Hyperscaler valuations have compressed this year and remain below post-pandemic peaks. Microsoft trades at about 24.6 times forward earnings, the highest of the group, while Meta trades at 17.6 times, the lowest.

"There are absolutely going to be fewer winners in the future than there likely are players today."

— Brian Barbetta, Wellington Management

What to Watch

Barbetta expects competition to narrow the field as the market matures, with those companies possessing the broadest technology portfolios, deepest customer relationships, and greatest control over their own infrastructure likely to pull ahead. For investors with exposure to Indian IT services firms riding the AI infrastructure wave, the message is similar: scale and customer lock-in will matter more than early positioning as the cycle matures.

The next test comes with the fall earnings season, when markets will be watching whether the promised cash-flow inflection begins to materialize — or whether the patience of even the most committed AI bulls starts to wear thin.
